text: Yo! Phone Memo here, also known as Babis. We're starting a show that
doesn't have a name yet. We'll figure it out along the way...
- We're here with Tzimos... - Yo!
We've worked on a release together, and he's the show's first guest!
To bring you into the concept, Tzimos:
this is a very DIY setup.
I want to document the whole creative process.
I want us to write together...
That's where we're going with this: building a beat together,
capturing everyone's input as we work through the process,
beyond the beats I make on my own. Whoever is in the room
gets to have a say, you know? - Okay.
I want to show what we can do with whatever we have,
however we can, to make music
and capture the whole process of writing verses.
Okay!
I want you to come in, make a beat with me, and write a verse over it!
- Right there, if possible... - Nice! - And record it.
We'll document all of it, so we end up with something good.
Okay. [censored] You've got a track with our friend,
Giannis, Nesom, who'll be on a future episode.
Spoilers! Spoilers! [calm down] In one line you say, "The definition of DIY."
- It's true! I inspired you! - You did inspire me, it's true.
- You say, "The definition of DIY." - Then I take it back and say
I'd rather do it with friends. - Okay. - Yeah.
- Exactly. - DIY with friends: "Do it yourselves," in the plural!
Okay. I understand DIY, "do it yourself,"
as creating or doing something with whatever I have right now,
or things I might acquire myself. I'm self-made. It's
"do it yourself." I want to show the struggle.
- You started rapping here in Heraklion? - Yeah.
- How did you start? - I started listening to rap in 2003.
We're not revealing our ages.
We won't say our ages. Go by how old we look.
I could've been listening since I was two! No, I was older.
I started with Imiskoumbria in 2003. - "Je suis Bossu?"
I wasn't good at French then... just like I'm not good at it now.
Specifically, "Greek Lover" was the first track. I think it was 2004.
- Ah, so you were good at English!
Good at English, obviously. Especially the English in "Greek Lover." Then
Goin' Through, and mostly Greek rap after that.
For international artists, I'd say Eminem.
- A lot of Eminem. - And in 2004, there was "Marshall Mathers"...
- No, the... - After "The Eminem Show." - Right! That's where I started.
Somehow I'd heard the melody of "Lose Yourself."
I knew I liked that music before I even knew what it was.
- Right. - Yeah.
- For me it was "When I'm Gone." - You're a little younger, then.
We're not revealing our ages! Still not revealing them.
You can see me on camera! Around fifth or sixth grade...
- I heard Goin' Through. - "We Want Vendetta." [rap beef reference]
Yeah, "We Want Vendetta"! No, that was later.
That was a little later. Goin' Through's "Vendetta," specifically.
I started writing my own stuff in my first year of secondary school.
- So, since 2007? - Yeah. Then we had Maskes.
Maskes was the crew I had with my school friends.
There was me, Ace on production, and
Doc producing too. Daz, later known as Abish, rapping, and Raid doing graffiti.
- So it was full-on hip-hop! - Full-on hip-hop, we felt it!
We were so hip-hop we didn't even know MSK, the tag we used, already existed
as a huge graffiti crew. - MSK is massive!
A massive graffiti crew. We also didn't know there was a Greek rock band
called Maskes, so we'd stolen everything without even knowing it!
So it doesn't count. - Great minds think alike!
I think the first YouTube comment was, "Don't you know there's
a Greek band called Maskes?" You joked about it, but you didn't know.
No! We didn't know. Sorry, it's all good!
We released our first record in 2014, called "Opou Mas Vgalei," because
we literally didn't know where it would take us. - You could tell!
- The name gave it away! - It didn't take us anywhere! Then we had one
called "I Vasi Mas." - Right. Let me tell you something, man.
Getting started is obviously tough. But you started
in secondary school, like I did. In my first year... or third year?
That summer I started producing too. There were forums,
all that stuff. I remember GR; I used to upload beats there.
Did you upload to GR, or just YouTube? - SoundCloud came first,
because it was easier: upload a WAV and see what happens.
How did you record? I literally had
a crappy computer hooked up to a Panasonic stereo. It was really funny,
with these huge speakers I obviously couldn't really use.
My mum would call out at home, telling me to turn the music up!
How was it for you? - We were lucky: Ace's cousin,
Nikitas, was in Indigo, a crew from Nea Alikarnassos. He'd already been
rapping for a few years, so they'd figured out how it worked.
- So there was rap in Heraklion. - There'd been rap here for ages.
Skonismenes Rimes, then Dirty South and the local crews. We can change the topic if you want.
I know all those. I just want to show there's rap in Heraklion.
There was rap in Heraklion, and there still is today. Got it. Let's say it again:
"There's rap in Heraklion."
I'll say it as often as you want until we believe it ourselves! So, with
their help, we recorded our first tracks. After that,
we wanted our own home studio. We didn't have money, just enough
for a night out at a place in Heraklion,
a little taverna. We drank two bottles of retsina and decided it was
a good time to head down to the beach by Xenia.
- Like any teenager would! - Yeah. In the alley behind the museum,
we look down and see a fifty-euro note. I pick it up, then
there's another fifty, then another fifty, and
a hundred!
We found €250 that night, just after we'd been saying,
"We want a studio too!"
The next day we bought a microphone, an audio interface, and headphones.
That's wild!
- We had a home studio! - Wild. The wildest thing we experienced as a crew.
- I wish everyone had your luck! - Obviously we took it as a
"meant to be" sign. We had to do something. We were much more creative then.
Then university, entrance exams, all of that...
- I'll come back to that too.
We drifted apart, but that's how we got started,
how we built the first home studio. - Entrance exams say it all!
Those things can hold you back from
growing as an artist. So many things can
get in the way of creativity and put it on pause. The EP we made together
is called "Reboot." - Right.
When we planned it, I said
it was a reboot for me too. I hadn't released anything for twelve years!
- Okay. - Apart from some
beat tapes I'd uploaded. Shout-out to Deectiva for agreeing
to do a beat tape with me before the EP. They didn't even sign me; we just said,
"Let's release something together." That was with MCD. It was fun. Shout-out to MCD!
How did you end up with the eight-year gap we mention on the EP?
My last release before this was an EP in 2017,
with Sonic Boom from Indigo, who I mentioned earlier,
produced by Ace. That was my last release, and after that,
personal stuff, health issues, family issues... one thing
led to another. A six-month break turned into
a year, then two. Suddenly I hadn't released
anything for about eight years. - Were you recording? - I wasn't writing much,
because I didn't have time. If I had written, I think I'd have found time
to record it. But because of all that
"I haven't got time," it was mostly an empty stretch.
Not much creativity. - How did you decide to start creating again?
- Good question. Just because I wasn't doing it doesn't mean
I didn't want to. Eventually I thought, "I have to
put this in my schedule." So I set aside two hours every day,
two hours working on music, whether anything came out of it or not.
Mostly to push myself to write, because
I needed it. I felt I wanted to do it. It's easy to make
excuses: "I'm busy, I haven't got time." But unless you make yourself do it,
it'll never happen. - Even this takes some organization.
Yeah. Meeting you helped a lot with that too.
- Really? - Yeah. I don't know if you remember how
we met. Shout-out to Stelios and EO. Stelios, our mutual friend,
introduced us: "This is Tzimos. He raps and wants a producer. This is Babis.
He produces and wants a rapper." That's how it happened. I went in
and listened to the beats. I especially liked "Sauce."
- "Sauce," man! - Which later became "SDE."
- Our hit! - The hit. We call it "Sauce" because,
according to Tzimos... I didn't know this... before recording,
you refer to the beat by its production name.
The rapper sees the name and sticks with it. It could be called "Nonsense 1,"
and you'd keep that. - If a beat is called "Nonsense 1,"
it stays "Nonsense 1" until it's uploaded and gets a title. Sometimes that becomes the title!
With Haris, Ace, we nearly
uploaded a track called "Ursula." I don't know why the beat was called that.
We almost hit upload.
The preview upload was called "Ursula." The track had nothing to do with any
Ursula! - Or an octopus, I'd imagine...
Nothing! Just before the final upload to YouTube,
we changed the name. - Yeah. The way I work...
I've got lots of ways of capturing ideas. I use an online DAW,
Soundtrap, which you don't like. Rumour has it
at least eighty percent of our tracks were made in
Soundtrap. - Yeah.
In your own creative process, is there a particular way
you write? Greek artists tend to move on from notebooks at some point.
Yeah. I generally prefer to have the beat first,
play it, and start writing. Because I work with
programming, and my lifestyle means I spend
a lot of time on a computer, it's much easier to write on
my keyboard than in a notebook. I'm slow at handwriting,
so when a thought comes, it's convenient to write it down straight away
and not lose it. I've lost countless lines. In the moment I thought,
"This is the best line ever!"
Then I didn't manage to write it down,
and it never came back. For one second it was the best line
ever written! So yes, beat first, then ideally
write on the computer, or on my phone.
Otherwise, my phone. The last time I wrote in a notebook
was when I couldn't use my phone or computer.
- In a cave! - Yeah, in a cave! My battery had died, and I had no
computer. That was last year, I think. Specifically, the second verse on
"Syntagi."
- Your favourite! - My favourite, I think.
It's better. Each track has its own thing, but I prefer it to "SDE."
For me, anyway. "Syntagi," with I Gut These. Let's give him
a shout-out! - Shout-out to I Gut These! All the shout-outs
we make... - We'll put them at the end!
Shout-out to: one, two...
Not there! Anyway, that's my way. I've got two questions
I'm asking for the first time, and I might ask future guests too,
because inspiration comes first. What's your
favourite line ever? And your favourite
song? They don't have to be the same. I'd like to ask your favourite rapper,
but I don't know if I want to. Like, "Please tell us
your favourite rapper later!" - Let me tell you my favourite too!
I don't know what answer we'll get, and then the comments will go,
[indistinct noises]
"Why do you like that guy?"
Because he's my favourite! It's subjective. Your favourite rapper could be anyone.
- Exactly. - Favourite line? You're killing me!
That's harder than picking a favourite track.
Let's go with a track. You're a rap encyclopedia; people don't
know that. A Greek-rap encyclopedia! - Greek-rap encyclopedia!
Someone asks you something, and you say, "Didn't you
know about that beef?" - Especially the beefs!
Let's move on from rap encyclopedia to Greek-rap gossip.
- Rap gossip, man! - I'm there for it, but I prefer the encyclopedia.
- Rap courts and rap gossip! - Yeah, something like that. So,
my favourite track is one I've mentioned for ages that not many people know.
That's a shame. I don't know if Teo will forgive me for always mentioning it.
It's "Vythos," by Logou Harin.
A track that... - That's deep! [Babis, stop trying to be funny]
It's been on YouTube for years, since 2017.
Yeah, around then. Maybe
earlier. - Of course, Teo has
newer music. He's just released a record.
He probably won't like me always talking about the old stuff. But yes,
my favourite is "Vythos," specifically the first verse. As for
a particular line... - If you can't pick one, let's go to the rapper.
Give me half a second to think. Put a timer here,
do something! I really don't know. There are
lines that stick with me for emotional reasons.
- Obviously. "Vythos" is quite an...
emotional track. - Yeah. Or it could be because
I really like technical rap. Something sticks with me
because I think, "How did he come up with that?"
- Technically, in the flow and the lyrics.
Yeah. Taking that as a good lead, I can't give you a
particular line, but my favourite MC would be Mikros Kleftis.
- Technically... - Exactly! His wordplay
is unmatched. - So your favourite MC is Greek?
- My favourite MC is Greek, yeah. - Nice.
I grew up on Greek hip-hop. I've also listened to lots of international music,
because you can't only listen to Greek rap.
- Obviously. - You can't make Greek
rap, only listen to Greek rap, and bring something new without
hearing things that aren't happening here. If you listen
only to Mikros Kleftis, you'll write like Mikros Kleftis.
That's a bigger
conversation. If you're doing something someone else does, you should do it
better. Taking somebody's style
and doing it better isn't necessarily bad. Either you do that,
or you do something new of your own, something different.
- Right. - The first option is
very difficult. It's hard to take Mikros Kleftis's style,
or Hatemost's... Which of Hatemost's styles would you even pick?
All of them! Asarkos, whoever it is, you'd have to do it better. These MCs
have years of experience; that style has already reached its peak.
It isn't easy to take someone's style
and improve it. - Especially Hatemost, who has loads of peaks!
Exactly. Making something new of your own,
you'll still have influences. They're there in everyone. In my case,
you can hear that I listen to MK in my tracks, because I've listened
to so much of his music that it's shaped who I am. Music
shapes you. - Yeah. If I rapped,
I'd probably be Taf Lathos. I've listened to so much of him...
Exactly. You'll make something of your own, but it'll be
influenced by the people who shaped you. Nothing can be
one hundred percent original, I think. Good luck to anyone who can do it!
Being original is great, but original doesn't necessarily mean good.
Anyway, let's not get into that. - This
conversation could go on for ages, but it's time,
given the weather and everything, to take you... For the first episode,
I thought we'd go up to the rooftop. Other episodes? I don't know
where we'll end up. We'll definitely go exploring, because it's fun
and I really like it. My place isn't a home
studio; it's my home. You'll see that in the footage. You'll also meet
Dias, my dog. I've found a really nice sample, a very repetitive sample,
and I know you like keeping things simple.
- Yeah, I like really simple stuff.
I thought, "Tzimos might like this sample."
- Nice. Let's check it out. - Let's go.
Let's go.

That's literally it.

I'm thinking of a glockenspiel
to give it a slightly eerie vibe. Play something...

It's funny that I've packed all these samples...

and I think you'll be sorted. I'm loading something from

It's fun. And the drums
go here.

Something more... for a hardcore feel,
something more direct. - Okay.

man, make a wish. Like a prayer, from your mouth to Kendrick's ear. It takes work,
work and a way to build something good. They know how to build from scratch.
No "don't," no "can't," cut ties with naysayers. With a beat from Babis, I don't
care what they say. You've got Barbie beside you; I've got lines that burn.
This is Rap Sta Bam, pure for the fam. Yours doesn't cut it, asshole; it's dead.
This style is rooted so deep in hip-hop, even if it dies, it stays standing.
Shirohige! Get up and leave, little man. Who told you off and suddenly invaded your space?
They ask me to drag it out. I want to beat them up. Everyone's talking, like we're at San Siro.
But I don't beat people up now that I'm grown, for better or worse, though I
did when I was little. No punches for a boxing bag; I've got punchlines to
feed you until you feel fat. Like me someday, maybe, but sorry,
that's a lie: I'm starting a diet on Monday. No New Era cap; I turn up with fresh air.
I don't want a Panamera; I want to take this further. That's why I push it and keep going
as long as I can, as long as I can stand it. Built my rap to destroy the beat. Some don't
like me, so I have to watch out. Because I take over every project
I'm on. Credit where it's due, fo' sho! Two lines inspired by Anser and Flow,
but I've come to steal the show. I devour a beat on the spot and
get two to go. Wassup! I'm not looking left or right. What everyone else does is none of my business.
I'm sure my turn will come. Took my ticket early; I'm at the front of the queue.
Don't get confused by similarities. I've got big plans, not cheap tricks.
I'm often the bad guy who starts it all. We fire it up and work on it every day.
Everyone to their own work; mine is urgent.
It isn't heard as much as it should be, and that injustice chokes me.
I don't want beef in the scene; I know how it ends. We're few but good; you're just few. That's how it ends.
That's it...
That was fun. A lot of fun!
